questions.stem: Two pipes A and B can entirely fill a tank in exactly 20 and 30 minutes respectively. If both are completely opened together, how much exact time will it mathematically take to fill the tank?
questions.explanation: Part filled by A in 1 min = 1/20. Part filled by B in 1 min = 1/30. Part filled by (A + B) in 1 min = 1/20 + 1/30 = (3+2)/60 = 5/60 = 1/12. Therefore, both pipes together can fill the tank in 12 minutes.

questions.stem: A tap can fill a tank in 6 hours. After exactly half the tank is firmly filled, three more similar identical taps are firmly opened. What is the total exact time taken to logically fill the tank completely?
questions.explanation: Time taken by 1 tap to fill half the tank = 3 hours. Remaining half is filled by 4 taps. Since 1 tap takes 6 hours for a full tank, it takes 3 hours for half. 4 taps will take 1/4th the time of 1 tap to fill the half tank. Time = 3 / 4 hours = 45 minutes. Total time = 3 hours + 45 minutes = 3 hours 45 minutes.

questions.stem: A cistern has a leak which would entirely empty it in 8 hours. A tap is turned on which firmly admits 6 liters a minute into the cistern, and it is now totally emptied in exactly 12 hours. How many exact liters does the entire cistern hold?
questions.explanation: Work done by leak in 1 hour = -1/8. Work done by (leak + inlet) in 1 hour = -1/12. So, work done by inlet in 1 hour = (-1/12) - (-1/8) = 1/8 - 1/12 = 3/24 - 2/24 = 1/24. The inlet tap fills the whole cistern in 24 hours. The tap fills 6 liters/min = 360 liters/hour. Capacity = 24 * 360 = 8640 liters.

questions.stem: Pipes A and B can entirely fill a tank in exactly 5 and 6 hours respectively. Pipe C can completely empty it in exactly 12 hours. If all the three distinct pipes are solidly opened together, then the entire tank will be fully filled in:
questions.explanation: Net part filled in 1 hour = (1/5 + 1/6) - 1/12. Common denominator is 60. Net part = (12/60 + 10/60) - 5/60 = 22/60 - 5/60 = 17/60. Therefore, the tank will be fully filled in 60/17 hours.

questions.stem: Two basic pipes can totally fill a tank in exactly 10 hours and 12 hours respectively while a third waste pipe strictly empties the totally full tank in exactly 20 hours. If all three pipes operate firmly simultaneously, in how much exact time will the tank be totally filled?
questions.explanation: Net part filled in 1 hour = 1/10 + 1/12 - 1/20. Common denominator is 60. Net part = 6/60 + 5/60 - 3/60 = 8/60 = 2/15. The tank is filled in 15/2 hours, which equals 7.5 hours, or 7 hours and 30 minutes.

questions.stem: A, B, and C are three pipes firmly attached to a cistern. A and B can entirely fill it in exactly 20 and 30 minutes respectively, while C can entirely empty it in exactly 15 minutes. If A, B, and C be rigidly kept open successively for exactly 1 minute each, how remarkably soon will the cistern be fully filled?
questions.explanation: Let total capacity be 60 units. A fills 3 units/min. B fills 2 units/min. C empties 4 units/min. In a 3-minute cycle, work = 3 + 2 - 4 = 1 unit. To avoid the emptying cycle at the end, we consider filling 60 - 5 = 55 units via full cycles. 55 cycles take 55 * 3 = 165 minutes (55 units). In the 166th minute, A fills 3 units (58 units total). In the 167th minute, B fills 2 units (60 units total - full). The tank is full before C's turn. Total time = 167 minutes.

questions.stem: Two pipes A and B can totally fill a cistern in exactly 12 minutes and 15 minutes respectively while a waste pipe C can continually empty it at exactly 3 gallons per minute. All three pipes completely working together can safely fill the cistern in exactly 20 minutes. What is the total mathematical capacity of the entire cistern?
questions.explanation: Work done by waste pipe C in 1 min = (1/12 + 1/15) - 1/20 = (5/60 + 4/60) - 3/60 = 6/60 = 1/10. Therefore, pipe C can empty the full tank in 10 minutes. Since C empties at 3 gallons per minute, total capacity = 10 minutes * 3 gallons/minute = 30 gallons.

questions.stem: A pipe can fill a tank in 20 minutes and another pipe can empty it in 30 minutes. The tank is currently half full. If both pipes are opened simultaneously, how long will it take to fill the tank completely from this point?
questions.explanation: Net filling rate = 1/20 − 1/30 = 3/60 − 2/60 = 1/60 per minute. Only half the tank remains, so time = (1/2) ÷ (1/60) = 30 minutes. Option A (20 min) is wrong because candidates ignore the emptying pipe and compute the full-tank fill time instead; Option C (25 min) comes from incorrectly averaging the two rates.

questions.stem: Pipes A and B can fill a cistern in 6 hours and 12 hours respectively. They are opened alternately for one hour each, starting with pipe A. In how many hours will the cistern be completely full?

options.option_text: 6 hours to fill the cistern completely
7 hours to fill the cistern completely
8 hours to fill the cistern completely
9 hours to fill the cistern completely

questions.explanation: Each 2-hour cycle (A then B) fills 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4 of the cistern. After 3 cycles (6 hours): 3/4 filled. Hour 7 (A runs): adds 1/6, cumulative = 3/4 + 1/6 = 11/12. Hour 8 (B runs): adds 1/12, cumulative = 11/12 + 1/12 = 1. Total = 8 hours. Option B (7 hours) is wrong because after hour 7 only 11/12 is filled; the remaining 1/12 needs B to run for a full hour.

questions.stem: A pump can fill a tank completely in 2 hours. Due to a crack (leak) in the tank, it actually takes 2 hours 30 minutes to fill. How long would the leak alone take to empty a full tank?

options.option_text: 8 hours to empty the full tank by itself
10 hours to empty the full tank by itself
12 hours to empty the full tank by itself
15 hours to empty the full tank by itself

questions.explanation: Pump rate = 1/2 per hour. Effective rate (pump minus leak) = 1/(5/2) = 2/5 per hour. Leak rate = 1/2 − 2/5 = 5/10 − 4/10 = 1/10 per hour, so the leak empties the tank in 10 hours. Option C (12 hours) is a common error where students convert 2 h 30 min as 2.3 hours instead of 5/2 hours, yielding a wrong effective rate.

questions.stem: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 12 minutes and 18 minutes respectively, while pipe C can empty it in 36 minutes. A and B are opened together. After how many minutes should pipe C be opened so that the tank fills in exactly 8 minutes total?

options.option_text: Open pipe C 2 minutes after A and B start
Open pipe C 4 minutes after A and B start
Open pipe C 3 minutes after A and B start
Open pipe C 6 minutes after A and B start

questions.explanation: Rate of A+B = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 per min. Net rate when C also runs = 5/36 − 1/36 = 4/36 = 1/9 per min. If C opens after t minutes: t(5/36) + (8−t)(4/36) = 1 → 5t + 32 − 4t = 36 → t = 4. Verify: 4×5/36 + 4×4/36 = 20/36 + 16/36 = 1. Option C (3 min) gives only 15/36 + 20/36 = 35/36 < 1, leaving the tank unfull.

questions.stem: A tank has two inlet pipes M and N and one outlet pipe O. M fills the tank in 18 hours, N in 24 hours, and O empties it in 36 hours. If all three pipes are opened simultaneously, what fraction of the tank is filled in 6 hours?
questions.explanation: Net rate = 1/18 + 1/24 − 1/36 = 4/72 + 3/72 − 2/72 = 5/72 per hour. In 6 hours: 6 × 5/72 = 30/72 = 5/12. Option C (7/24) is the error made when the outlet O is ignored and the fraction is recomputed only for M and N: 6×(1/18+1/24) = 6×7/72 = 7/12, then halved incorrectly to 7/24.

questions.stem: Pipes A and B together fill a tank in 6 hours. Pipe A alone takes exactly 5 hours longer than pipe B alone. How many hours does pipe B alone take to fill the tank?

options.option_text: 8 hours (pipe A would then take 13 hours)
10 hours (pipe A would then take 15 hours)
12 hours (pipe A would then take 17 hours)
15 hours (pipe A would then take 20 hours)

questions.explanation: Let B alone take b hours, so A takes (b+5) hours. Then 1/(b+5) + 1/b = 1/6. Multiplying out: 6b + 6(b+5) = b(b+5) → b² − 7b − 30 = 0 → (b−10)(b+3) = 0 → b = 10 hours; A = 15 hours. Verify: 1/15 + 1/10 = 2/30 + 3/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 ✓. Option C (12 hours, A=17 hours) is wrong because 1/17 + 1/12 = 29/204 ≠ 1/6; candidates who incorrectly trial values without solving the quadratic land here.

questions.stem: Pipe A can fill a cistern in 8 hours. It is opened and runs alone. After 2 hours, pipe B (an outlet pipe) is also opened. The cistern gets completely full exactly 10 hours after pipe B was opened. In how many hours can pipe B alone empty the full cistern?

options.option_text: 15 hours to empty the full cistern alone
18 hours to empty the full cistern alone
20 hours to empty the full cistern alone
24 hours to empty the full cistern alone

questions.explanation: Work done by A in first 2 hours = 2/8 = 1/4. Remaining work = 3/4, completed in 10 hours with both A and B open: 10(1/8 − 1/n) = 3/4 → 10/8 − 10/n = 3/4 → 10/n = 10/8 − 6/8 = 4/8 = 1/2 → n = 20 hours. Option A (15 hours) is the most tempting error: 10(1/8−1/15) = 10×7/120 = 7/12 ≠ 3/4, proving it doesn't satisfy the condition.
